skills.name: Ionic bonding: formation and formulae of ionic compounds

note.text:
In ionic bonding, a metal atom transfers electrons to a non-metal atom:
• Na (2,8,1) loses 1 → Na⁺ (2,8); Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 → Cl⁻ (2,8,8). The ions attract: NaCl.
• Mg (2,8,2) loses 2 → Mg²⁺; O (2,6) gains 2 → O²⁻: MgO.
Dot-and-cross diagrams show the outer electrons of each atom (dots for one, crosses for the other) and the charges of the ions.
Formula: the total positive charge must equal the total negative charge. Mg²⁺ with Cl⁻ needs two Cl⁻: MgCl₂. Al³⁺ with O²⁻: Al₂O₃.

sections.heading: Transferring electrons
sections.text:
When a metal meets a non-metal, the metal atom gives its outer electrons to the non-metal atom.
Sodium ({2},{8},{1}) gives its one outer electron to chlorine ({2},{8},{7}). Now sodium is Na⁺ ({2},{8}) and chlorine is Cl⁻ ({2},{8},{8}): both have full shells.
The positive and negative ions attract each other strongly. This attraction is the ionic bond.

sections.heading: Dot-and-cross diagrams
sections.text:
To show the transfer, draw the outer shells only: the metal's electrons as crosses (×) and the non-metal's as dots (•).
After the transfer, draw each ion in square brackets with its charge outside, for example [Na]⁺ and [Cl]⁻ with eight electrons around chlorine.
Remember: electrons move from the metal to the non-metal, never the other way.

sections.heading: Writing formulae
sections.text:
An ionic compound has no overall charge, so the charges must balance.
• Na⁺ and Cl⁻: one of each, NaCl.
• Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻: two chlorides, MgCl₂.
• Al³⁺ and O²⁻: lowest common multiple {6}, so two Al and three O: Al₂O₃.
Use the smallest whole numbers that balance.

key_words.meaning: a drawing of outer electrons showing transfer or sharing
a giant regular arrangement of positive and negative ions

mistake.wrong: Chlorine gives an electron to sodium
mistake.right: Sodium (the metal) gives an electron to chlorine
mistake.why: Metals lose electrons; non-metals gain them.

worked_example.problem: Show how aluminium and oxygen form an ionic compound, and give its formula.
steps: Al ({2},{8},{3}) loses {3} electrons → Al³⁺. O ({2},{6}) gains {2} → O²⁻.
Charges must balance: the lowest common multiple of {3} and {2} is {6}.
Two Al³⁺ give +{6}; three O²⁻ give −{6}.

cards.idea: The metal loses electrons and the non-metal gains them.
Balance the charges to get the formula.

pick.q: When magnesium reacts with oxygen, what ions form?
e: Magnesium loses two electrons and oxygen gains two.
The metal becomes positive, the non-metal negative.
Oxygen gains two electrons, not one.

pick.q: In sodium chloride, what is the electron arrangement of the chloride ion?
e: Chloride gains one electron, giving 18 in all.

pick.q: What holds the ions together in an ionic compound?

cards.idea: The ions attract because they have opposite charges.
example: {'Na⁺'} and {'Cl⁻'} pack together in a giant lattice.

questions.prompt: What is the formula of {compoundName(X.p, X.n)}?

misconceptions.explain: One of each does not balance +{valency(X.p)} and −{valency(X.n)}.
The numbers are the wrong way round: the number of {X.n} comes from the charge of {X.p}.
Use the smallest whole numbers that balance the charges.

solution: {X.p} forms an ion of charge +{valency(X.p)}; {X.n} forms an ion of charge −{valency(X.n)}.

questions.prompt: How many electrons does each {nameOf(P)} atom transfer when it forms an ionic compound?

misconceptions.explain: Metals lose their few outer electrons; they do not gain.

solution: It transfers all {answer} to the non-metal.

questions.prompt: In the formula of {compoundName(P, N)}, how many {nameOf(N)} ions are there for each formula unit? (Give the number of {N} in the formula.)

misconceptions.explain: The number of {N} comes from the metal's charge (+{valency(P)}).

solution: Formula {formula(compoundFormula(P, N))}: there are {answer} {N} in it.
where: valency(P) / hcf(valency(P), valency(N)) != valency(N) / hcf(valency(P), valency(N))

questions.prompt: Put the steps of forming sodium chloride in order.

items.text: The sodium atom (2, 8, 1) loses its outer electron.
The chlorine atom (2, 8, 7) gains that electron.
Na⁺ (2, 8) and Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8) are formed, each with a full outer shell.
The oppositely charged ions attract to form an ionic lattice.

questions.hint: Start with the metal losing its electron.
